He had, in fact, no idea of his own power over her feelings. When he followed her into the shrubbery, he had not meant to test it. He had come because he was anxious to know how she was coping with Frank Churchill’s engagement. He had no selfish purpose, no intention beyond offering comfort or advice if she gave him the chance. Everything else happened on the impulse of the moment, as what he heard affected his feelings. Her welcome assurance that she cared nothing for Frank Churchill, that her heart was entirely free of him, awakened a hope that he might eventually win her love himself. But he had not hoped to win it immediately. In a moment when eagerness overcame judgment, he had wanted only permission to try. The greater hopes that gradually emerged were all the more wonderful. The love he had been asking to earn, if he could, was already his. In half an hour, he had gone from deep distress to something so close to perfect happiness that no other name would fit.

Her change was just as great. That same half hour gave each the precious certainty of being loved and removed an equal burden of ignorance, jealousy, or doubt. His jealousy had existed for a long time, since Frank Churchill’s arrival or even the expectation of it. He had loved Emma and been jealous of Frank for about the same length of time; one feeling had probably helped him recognize the other. Jealousy had driven him away from the country. The gathering at Box Hill finally made him decide to leave. He wanted to spare himself another sight of Frank’s attentions being accepted and encouraged. He went away hoping to learn indifference, but chose the wrong place. His brother’s home contained too much domestic happiness. Womanhood appeared too lovable there, and Isabella resembled Emma too closely. Her differences were only obvious shortcomings that made Emma shine more brightly by comparison. Even a longer stay could have achieved little. Still, he stubbornly remained, day after day, until that morning’s mail brought the news of Jane Fairfax. He felt the happiness anyone would have felt, and felt no shame in it, since he had never considered Frank Churchill worthy of Emma. But alongside that joy came such tender concern and such intense anxiety for her that he could stay away no longer. He rode home through the rain and walked over directly after dinner to see how this sweetest and best of women—faultless despite all her faults—was bearing the discovery.

When I review the terrible list of my sins, I can hardly believe I am the same creature whose mind once held such glorious visions of goodness, beauty, and greatness. But it is true: the fallen angel becomes a vicious devil. Yet even that enemy of God and humanity had companions in his misery. I have no one.

“You, who call Frankenstein your friend, seem to know my crimes and his suffering. But his account could not convey the hours and months of misery I endured, wasting away with feelings I could not satisfy. Destroying his hopes did nothing to fulfill my own desires. They remained fierce and hungry. I still wanted love and companionship, and people still rejected me. Was that not unjust? Must I be the only criminal when all humanity wronged me? Why do you not hate Felix, who insulted his friend and drove him from the door? Why do you not curse the countryman who tried to kill the one who saved his child? No, they are good and blameless! I, miserable and abandoned, am a malformed thing to be rejected, kicked, and trampled. Even now, remembering that injustice makes my blood boil.

“But I am indeed a wicked creature. I have killed the beautiful and the defenseless. I have strangled innocent people in their sleep and crushed the throat of someone who had never harmed me or any living thing. I condemned my creator—a man who embodied all that deserves love and admiration—to misery. I pursued him until he reached this final, irreversible ruin. There he lies, pale and cold in death. You hate me, but your disgust cannot equal my own. I look at the hands that carried out these acts and think of the heart that imagined them. I long for the moment when I will no longer see these hands, when those terrible thoughts will no longer haunt me.

“Do not fear that I will cause further harm. My work is almost finished. Neither your death nor anyone else’s is needed to complete my existence and accomplish what remains. Only my own is required. Do not suppose I will delay this sacrifice. I will leave your ship on the ice raft that brought me here and travel to the northernmost point of the world. There I will build my funeral fire and burn this wretched body to ashes. Its remains must teach nothing to some curious, unholy person who might try to create another creature like me.

But enough of that. I will begin my story. It is my final task, and I hope I am strong enough to complete it. I have no crimes to confess. My faults should be easily forgiven, since they came from poor judgment rather than bad intentions. I believe few people would claim that wiser choices or different behavior could have saved them from the misfortunes I have suffered. My life has been ruled by necessity, a horrible necessity. Breaking the thick, unyielding chain that bound me would have required stronger hands than mine—stronger, I believe, than any human hands. I once lived only for joy, filled with warm love and delight in goodness. That chain fastened me to misery that can end only in death, and now soon will. But I am forgetting myself; I have not yet told my story. I will stop for a moment, wipe my clouded eyes, and try to lose this vague but heavy unhappiness in the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of high rank. His own father died when he was young, and a weak mother raised him with all the indulgence she thought a wealthy nobleman deserved. He went to Eton and then to college. From childhood he could freely spend large sums of money, so he enjoyed the independence that such advantages always give a boy at a public boarding school.

These circumstances provided rich ground for his passions to take root and grow, whether they naturally grew as flowers or weeds. Always allowed to make his own choices, he developed a strong, distinct character early. An observant person could have seen in its variety the beginnings of both virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance led him to spend enormous sums on passing whims. Because these whims felt so powerful, he honored them with the name of passions. This extravagance often took the form of limitless generosity. Yet while he sincerely attended to other people’s needs, his own wishes were fully satisfied as well. He gave money, but sacrificed none of his desires by doing so. He gave time, which he did not consider valuable, and affection, which he was glad to exercise in any way.

I do not mean that he would have been unusually selfish if his wishes had competed with someone else’s. That test simply never came. He grew up surrounded by prosperity and all its benefits. Everyone loved him and wanted to make him happy.
